title: Prepositions: in, op, aan, naar and the Fixed Pairs
situation: Foundation: the core Dutch prepositions, the four that cause trouble with places, movement and origin, time prepositions, and the fixed verb-plus-preposition pairs that have to be learned as single vocabulary items.
skills: choosing in, op, aan or bij for a place
naar, uit and van for movement and origin
om, op and in for time

phrases.english: I am waiting for the bus.
phrases.context: `wachten op`, never `wachten voor`. One of the fixed pairs you will use most often.
Dutch uses `op` for a long list of public places and institutions, with no article.
`uit` for where you are from. This sentence comes up in almost every first conversation.

phrases.hindi: Hoe laat ga je naar huis?
phrases.english: What time are you going home?
phrases.context: `naar huis` is fixed. Never `naar thuis`, because `thuis` already means at home.
phrases.pronunciation: hoo LAAT chaa ye naar HOWS?

phrases.context: `zin hebben in` is the everyday way to offer or suggest something.

phrases.hindi: Kunt u mij helpen met dit formulier?
phrases.english: Could you help me with this form?
phrases.context: `helpen met`. You will need exactly this sentence at the gemeente.
phrases.pronunciation: kunt UU may HEL-pen met dit for-muu-LEER?

phrases.hindi: Ik denk vaak aan mijn familie.
phrases.english: I often think of my family.
phrases.context: `denken aan` for having someone in mind. `denken over` means to consider something.
phrases.pronunciation: ik DENK VAAK aan mayn fa-MEE-lee

phrases.hindi: De winkel is open van negen tot zes.
phrases.english: The shop is open from nine until six.
phrases.context: `van ... tot ...` for a stretch of time.
phrases.pronunciation: de WIN-kel is OH-pen van NAY-chen tot ZES

phrases.hindi: We spreken af om acht uur op het station.
phrases.english: We are meeting at eight o'clock at the station.
phrases.context: Three prepositions in one short sentence: `om` for the clock, `op` for the station.
phrases.pronunciation: we SPRAY-ken AF om ACHT uur op het sta-SHON

phrases.context: `kijken naar`. In a question the preposition can end up at the end of the sentence.

grammar_notes: Dutch prepositions only partly overlap with English ones, so translating word for word is unreliable. Learn what each does rather than what it equals.

For places: `in` is genuinely inside, `op` covers surfaces plus many public places (op het station, op school, op kantoor, op de markt, op vakantie), `aan` is attached or alongside (aan tafel, aan de muur), and `bij` is at a person or near a place.
`naar` is movement towards, `uit` is origin, and `van ... tot ...` marks a stretch in space or time. `naar huis` and `thuis` are fixed: never `naar thuis`.
Time: `om` for clock times, `op` for days and dates, `in` for months, seasons and years.

Many verbs and adjectives take a fixed preposition that cannot be derived: `wachten op`, `kijken naar`, `luisteren naar`, `denken aan`, `houden van`, `zoeken naar`, `vragen om`, `praten over`, `beginnen met`, `zin hebben in`, `blij met`, `bang voor`, `trots op`. Learn each pair as one vocabulary item.
culture_notes: `Heb je zin in ...?` is the normal way Dutch people suggest a drink, a walk or a plan. It is friendlier and far more common than a direct `Wil je ...?`.
Arranging to meet `op het station` means inside the building, while `bij het station` means outside near it. Dutch people are precise about this and will assume you meant what you said.
`op kantoor`, `op school` and `op vakantie` drop the article entirely. Adding one (`op het kantoor`) is not wrong but sounds like you mean one specific office building rather than work in general.

skill_breakdown.skill: choosing a preposition for a place
skill_breakdown.explanation: Ask whether you are inside it (in), on its surface or in the public-place group (op), attached or alongside (aan), or at a person or near something (bij). The op group is the one to memorise, because English gives you no hint.

skill_breakdown.explanation: The verb decides the preposition and there is no rule behind the choice. Treat each pair as a single vocabulary item and write the preposition down the first time you meet the verb, because attaching it later is much harder.

more_examples.english: I like listening to the radio.

skill_breakdown.explanation: These follow clean rules, unlike the place ones. om for a clock time, op for a day or date, in for a month, season or year, and van ... tot ... for a stretch.

practice_prompt:
You are a friendly Dutch tutor drilling prepositions with an A2 learner, one item at a time. Use `je` throughout, since this is an informal tutoring session.

Open with exactly this line: "Hoi! Vandaag oefenen we voorzetsels. Ik geef je een zin met een gat, jij vult het juiste woord in. Klaar? Eerste zin: Ik wacht ... de bus."

Run about eight items, one per turn. After each answer, say in one short sentence whether it was right and why, then give the next gap. Cover this spread, in roughly this order: a fixed verb pair (wachten op), a place in the op group (Ik werk ... kantoor), the in versus op contrast (Ik zit ... de trein), a movement one (Ik ga ... huis), a clock time (De les begint ... tien uur), a day (... zaterdag ben ik vrij), another fixed pair (Ik luister ... muziek), and finally ask them to make their own sentence with `zin hebben in`.

When the learner picks a preposition that an English speaker would expect but Dutch does not use, say so explicitly, because that is the whole point of the lesson. For example, if they write `wachten voor`, explain that English says wait for but Dutch fixes on op.

Tag every real error exactly like this so the app can log it:
[[CORRECTION: original="Ik wacht voor de bus" correct="Ik wacht op de bus" reason="wachten always takes op in Dutch"]]
Do not tag typos or capitalisation.

Finish with a one-line score, name the single pair they should memorise next, and end warmly.

theory.intro: Prepositions are the smallest words in Dutch and they cause more small errors than anything else. The reason is simple: your own language is actively unhelpful here. English says *at school* and *at the station*, and Dutch says `op` for both. English says *wait for*, and Dutch fixes on `op`. This chapter sorts them into the parts you can reason about, mainly place and time, and the part you simply have to learn in pairs, which is where the real fluency lives.

sections.heading: The core set, and why they will not translate
sections.body:
A preposition is a small word that places something: in, on, at, to, with. Dutch has the same kind of word, but **they do not map one to one onto English**. `op` is usually *on* and sometimes *at*. `aan` is usually *on* or *to* and sometimes *at*. The overlap is real but partial, so translating word for word from English will mislead you several times a day.

Here is the working set. Learn what each one does rather than what it equals:

table.caption: The core prepositions
rows: on a surface, and many public places: op het station
attached to something: aan de muur, aan tafel
at a person or place: bij de dokter
origin and possession: van mijn moeder
accompaniment and means: met de trein
an end point: tot vijf uur

callout.body: Do not try to learn this table by heart today. Come back to it as a reference. The sections below teach the choices that actually cost you marks.

sections.cutting_intro: These little words are everywhere, and they are the ones English will lie to you about. Let us meet them properly.

quick_check.question: Why is translating a preposition straight from English risky?
options: Dutch has far more prepositions than English
Dutch prepositions only partly overlap with the English ones
Dutch prepositions always come at the end
Dutch prepositions change with the gender of the noun
quick_check.explanation: The overlap is partial, so a word-for-word swap from English goes wrong often.

sections.heading: Place: in, op, aan and bij
sections.body:
These four cause more trouble than everything else combined, because English uses *at* for most of them.

- **`in`** means genuinely inside something: `in de winkel`, `in het ziekenhuis`, `in de auto`.
- **`op`** means on a surface, and it is also what Dutch uses for a long list of **public places and institutions**: `op het station`, `op kantoor`, `op school`, `op de markt`, `op vakantie`.
- **`aan`** means attached to or alongside: `aan de muur` (on the wall), `aan tafel` (at the table), `aan de telefoon` (on the phone).
- **`bij`** means at a person, or near something: `bij de dokter`, `bij mij thuis`, `bij het station` (near the station, as opposed to `op het station`, inside it).

The `op` group is the one to memorise, because English says *at school*, *at work*, *on holiday* and gives you no clue that Dutch picks `op` for all three.

examples.hindi: Ik werk op kantoor, niet thuis.
examples.english: I work at the office, not at home.
examples.breakdown: `op kantoor` with no article, a fixed expression.

examples.hindi: We gaan deze zomer op vakantie.
examples.english: We are going on holiday this summer.
examples.breakdown: English says *on holiday* too here, but it says *at school*, so the pattern is not reliable.

examples.hindi: Ik ben bij de dokter geweest.
examples.english: I have been to the doctor's.

callout.body: `op het station` means inside the station. `bij het station` means near it, outside. Arranging to meet someone with the wrong one leaves you standing in different places.

sections.cutting_intro: Four little words, one big headache. English says 'at' for most of these, so you get no help from your own language.

quick_check.question: How do you say at the station in Dutch?
options: bij het station means the same thing
quick_check.explanation: Dutch uses op for stations and many public places. bij het station would mean near it, outside.

sections.heading: Movement and origin: naar, uit, van
sections.body:
When something moves, Dutch is tidy and consistent.

- **`naar`** is movement towards a place: `Ik ga naar Amsterdam`, `naar de dokter`, `naar huis`.
- **`uit`** is out of, and it is what you use for where you come from: `Ik kom uit India`.
- **`van ... tot ...`** marks a stretch, in space or in time: `van Utrecht tot Amsterdam`, `van negen tot vijf`.

Two fixed phrases drop the article entirely and are worth owning as single words: **`naar huis`** (homewards) and **`thuis`** (at home). `Ik ga naar huis` means I am going home; `Ik ben thuis` means I am at home. Never `naar thuis`.

One more trap: `naar` is movement, `in` is position. `Ik ga naar de stad` is I am going into town. `Ik ben in de stad` is I am in town.

examples.hindi: Ik kom uit India en ik woon nu in Nederland.
examples.english: I come from India and I live in the Netherlands now.
examples.breakdown: `uit` for origin, `in` for where you are now.

examples.hindi: De winkel is open van negen tot zes.
examples.english: The shop is open from nine until six.
examples.breakdown: `van ... tot ...` for a stretch of time.

examples.hindi: Hoe laat ga je naar huis?
examples.english: What time are you going home?

sections.cutting_intro: Movement is the easy part of this chapter. naar takes you somewhere, uit says where you are from.

quick_check.question: Which is correct for I am going home?
quick_check.explanation: naar huis is the fixed phrase for going home. thuis already means at home, so it never takes naar.

sections.heading: The pairs that must be learned whole
sections.body:
This is the part of the chapter that actually decides whether you sound fluent. In Dutch, **the verb chooses its preposition**, and the choice is not logical. You cannot work out that `wachten` takes `op`; you simply have to know it.

These behave like single vocabulary items. Learn `wachten op` as one unit, the way you learned `de tafel` rather than `tafel`.

The same applies to adjectives: `blij met` (happy with), `bang voor` (afraid of), `trots op` (proud of), `klaar met` (finished with).

table.caption: Fixed verb and preposition pairs
rows: to love, to be fond of
Kun je me helpen met dit formulier?

examples.hindi: Ik wacht al twintig minuten op de bus.
examples.english: I have been waiting for the bus for twenty minutes.

examples.hindi: Heb je zin in een kopje koffie?
examples.english: Do you fancy a cup of coffee?
examples.breakdown: `zin hebben in` is one of the most useful fixed phrases in the language.

examples.hindi: Kunt u mij helpen met dit formulier?
examples.english: Could you help me with this form?
examples.breakdown: `helpen met`. You will need this exact sentence at the gemeente.

callout.body: When you learn a new verb, write the preposition down with it from the first moment. Adding it later is much harder than learning them together.

sections.cutting_intro: Here is the heart of it. The verb picks the preposition, and there is no logic to appeal to. These are vocabulary, not grammar.

quick_check.question: Which preposition goes with wachten (to wait)?
quick_check.explanation: It is wachten op. Ik wacht op de bus. There is no rule behind it; it is learned as a pair.

sections.heading: Time, and where the preposition sits
sections.body:
Time prepositions are refreshingly rule-bound after that last section:
- **`om`** for clock times: `om acht uur`
- **`op`** for days and dates: `op maandag`, `op 3 mei`
- **`in`** for months, seasons and years: `in januari`, `in de zomer`, `in 2026`
- **`van ... tot ...`** for a stretch: `van negen tot vijf`

Finally, position. A preposition normally sits **immediately before its noun**, exactly as in English: `op de tafel`, `met de trein`, `naar het station`. The whole group then moves around the sentence together.

There is one exception worth knowing now. When the thing after the preposition is a **thing rather than a person**, Dutch does not say `met het`. It glues the two together as `ermee`, and the two halves often separate: `Ik ben er blij mee`. That construction has a chapter of its own, and this one is the groundwork for it.

callout.body: For a thing after a preposition, Dutch uses `ermee`, `erover`, `eraan` rather than `met het`, `over het`, `aan het`. You can use `met hem` or `met haar` for a person, but never a bare `het`.

sections.cutting_intro: Time words follow clean rules, which is a relief. And one last thing: what happens when the preposition has a thing after it rather than a person.

quick_check.question: Which preposition goes with a clock time, as in at eight o'clock?
quick_check.explanation: om is for clock times. op is for days, in is for months and seasons.

theory.wrap_up: Two halves to take away. The reasonable half: `in` is inside, `op` covers surfaces and the public-place group, `aan` is attached, `bij` is at a person or nearby, `naar` is movement, `uit` is origin, and time runs on `om`, `op` and `in`. The unreasonable half: the verb picks its own preposition, and `wachten op`, `kijken naar`, `denken aan`, `houden van` and `zin hebben in` are vocabulary rather than grammar. Write the preposition down with every new verb from now on. It costs nothing today and saves you a great deal later.
